title: Cross-SDK stream + tool calling + typed structured-output examples and compatibility shim
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background: Customers have asked for clearer cross-language guidance and drop-in examples for progressive adoption of streaming responses, first-class tool/function calling, and structured outputs. We currently expose these features in the runtime and API, but the language SDKs have diverged in surface area and examples. This ticket proposes a minimal set of API patterns and concrete code samples for TypeScript, Python, and Go, plus a lightweight compatibility shim that allows OpenAI-like callsites to work with Redwood's typed tool schema.

Goals:
- Define a consistent streaming event model and streaming iterator pattern across SDKs.
- Provide canonical function/tool calling semantics (declaration, verification, execution hooks) plus automatic JSON schema parsing for structured outputs.
- Ship a small compatibility layer (openai-compat) to accept legacy params and translate to Redwood SDK idioms so customers can migrate with small code changes.
- Deliver cross-language examples (TS/py/go) in the repo and add to quickstarts.

Scope and deliverables:
1) Spec doc (link below) defining: streaming events, partial delta merges, error framing, tool call request/response envelope, and structured output validation semantics.
2) TypeScript SDK updates:
   - streaming() returns AsyncIterable<StreamEvent> with unified types for delta/token/structured-chunk/tool-call.
   - tool definitions typed with zod-compatible runtime validators and TypeScript types.
   - example: incremental parse of structured output + type-safe tool invocation helper.
3) Python SDK updates:
   - async generator for streaming with explicit event classes (Delta, ToolCall, SchemaChunk, Final).
   - dataclass-based tool schemas and pydantic validation helpers.
   - example notebook that shows how to run tool sandboxing in an async web handler.
4) Go SDK updates:
   - channel-based stream model with StreamEvent interface and helper parsers.
   - codegen option that emits Go structs from JSON schema for structured outputs.
5) openai-compat shim:
   - adapter that accepts OpenAI-compatible "function_call" style parameters and maps them to Redwood tool schema.
   - runtime flags to enable/disable auto-conversion and legacy param warnings.
6) Tests and CI:
   - unit tests for streaming shapes and schema parsing, cross-language golden examples, and integration smoke tests against a Redwood dev cluster.

Design artifacts and links:
- Design doc (internal): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/SDK+Crosswalk+Streaming+Tool+Schema+Spec
- Example PR (WIP): https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/329
- UX sample app showing tool orchestration: drive:example-apps/sdk-tooling-demo

Non-goals:
- Full codegen for all languages in this ticket (we'll provide a minimal codegen hook for Go; broader codegen tracked elsewhere).
- Rewriting existing SDK internals — this is additive surface and adapter layer only.

Acceptance criteria:
- TS/py/go example snippets merged into /examples and referenced in quickstarts.
- openai-compat shim available behind feature flag; documentation included.
- Unit tests covering streaming events and at least 2 structured-schema parsing cases per language.
- Docs and migration guide live in docs/sdk/compatibility.
comments: 2025-01-20 — Initial spike completed. Prototyped TS AsyncIterable and Python async generator. Discovered inconsistency in how 'tool_call' partial events were emitted (TS emitted full params only on final event; Python had incremental args). Team decision: emit tool_call start + arg_delta chunks + tool_call_complete for parity.

2025-01-23 — Design review with PM/Docs. Agreed to use explicit event types rather than relying on string tags to make cross-language parsing robust. Action: Alejandro to draft TS types and json-schema->pydantic helper.

2025-01-28 — PR #329 opened with TypeScript streaming helper and example. Needs test coverage and review from SDK-Infra. Owen Liu volunteered to review for performance implications of streaming parse. (link in description)

2025-01-31 — Go prototype shows a small GC pressure for naive JSON-decoding for each token. Decided to use incremental json.Decoder with pooled buffers in the Go helper. Assigned to Priya Kaur to implement and benchmark.

2025-02-03 — Security reviewed shim design; no secrets leakage concerns. Need to ensure openai-compat warns when using legacy params (audit requirement). Docs task created for compliance team to sign off on messaging.
2025-02-03 — Next steps: finalize tests, merge TS and Python helpers, land go-channel parser behind feature flag. Schedule canary rollout in SDK-2.4.0 cycle.
notes_for_reviewers:
Key trade-offs: (1) Strict typed parsing vs developer ergonomics — we favor explicit validation with opt-out to keep production reliability high. (2) Compatibility shim may hide breaking behavior; it should be opt-in and log warnings. Please review the shim's mapping table in the design doc.

Testing notes: include load test with streaming enabled and tool-call heavy workload (tool calls per 100 tokens). Ensure memory usage matches baseline within 15%.
migration_instructions: - For OpenAI-compatible callers: enable 'openai_compat: true' in SDK client config and add a migration flag to the request. - For TypeScript users: replace usage of client.streamRaw with client.streamTyped and use 'for await (const ev of stream)' to handle StreamEvent types. - For Python users: switch from client.stream_tokens() to 'async for ev in client.stream()' and use provided pydantic models. - For Go users: use client.NewStream(ctx) and read from Stream.EventChan(); call schemagen to emit structs if desired.
